title: Controversy
hookLine: in the 1230s some banned and burned his books

lines: WHAT CAME OUT THE OTHER SIDE.
cards: Open a printed Mishneh Torah to a page of its Book of Knowledge and look at the margins. Next to Maimonides' clean Hebrew sit other voices, in smaller type. Some explain him.
Some defend him. A few say, more or less, he's wrong. The book that became a pillar of Jewish learning started out in a fight.
In his own lifetime people accused him. After his death, some rabbis banned his philosophical writings, and accounts tell of copies being burned.

teach.b: Controversy. First, the accusation. While Maimonides was alive, some readers said his code barely spoke about the resurrection of the dead, and wondered whether he believed in it.
He answered with a whole essay: yes, he did, and it already stood in his own list of principles. A man known for clarity had to explain himself.

teach.h: THE RABAD'S NOTES IN THE MARGIN.
teach.b: Second, the critic in the margin. A scholar in Provence, Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp notes on the code.
Where Maimonides calls anyone who imagines God with a body a heretic, the Rabad objects: greater and better people than that, he writes, held such a view, misled by the plain words of verses.
He isn't saying God has a body. He's saying don't call sincere people heretics. Those notes are printed right beside the code.
Third, the fire. After Maimonides died, a bitter dispute broke out over his philosophy.
Some rabbis feared the Guide and the Book of Knowledge would lead readers away from simple faith, and banned their study. Others defended him just as fiercely.
Accounts say his books were burned; historians still argue over exactly who did what. Fourth, then canon.

teach.h: FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN, IT ENDURES.
teach.b: An argument for the sake of heaven, says the Mishnah, will endure, like the arguments of Hillel and Shammai. The banned books stayed on the shelf. His principles went into the prayer book.
The critic and the criticized now share a page.
Controversy didn't erase him. It became part of how he is read.

how: Printed editions of the Mishneh Torah carry commentaries around the text, including the Rabad's critical notes, so disagreement is part of the page students study.

o: a public debate he won outright while still alive
the fight over Maimonides' books that left them central

games.q: you're a scholar reading Maimonides' new code, and one line goes too far for you: it calls sincere people heretics. what do you do?
o: write your objection beside his words.
call for the book to be burned.
games.why: the Rabad wrote sharp notes on the code. those notes are printed right beside it, so readers still hear both voices.

practice: Bring to mind a thinker, writer or teacher you've argued with, out loud or in your head, and keep the disagreement just as it is. Next to it, find one thing that person saw clearly, one sentence of credit.
Then picture the two of you on a single page, your note in the margin beside their words, both kept.

wordCard.voice: Controversy. In Hebrew, machloket. For Maimonides it meant accusation, critique and even burned books, and then a place at the center of Jewish learning. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: dispute or controversy; Pirkei Avot speaks of a machloket for the sake of heaven that endures.

carryVoice: Your line: controversy, then canon. An argument for the sake of heaven lasts. See you tomorrow.
